extracted.intended_audience: general readers, policymakers, and anyone concerned with freedom of opinion and public discussion
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and evaluative principles about when and why opinions should be freely discussed rather than suppressed; addresses both individual intellectual practice and public/political justification for toleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrigibility of error
rubrics_metrics.description: Human errors are corrigible; the capacity to rectify mistakes by discussion and experience is the source of intellectual and moral progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts alone rarely tell their own story; discussion is needed to interpret experience. The reliability of human judgment depends on preserving the means of correction (discussion, criticism, exposure to counterargument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep means of correction constantly at hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Society must maintain continual opportunities for criticism and counterargument so that errors can be revealed and corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'means of setting [judgment] right' must be kept available; otherwise confidence in public judgment is misplaced. Institutionalized practices (e.g., allowing challenges, debate) are necessary safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to criticism as a marker of trustworthy judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A person whose judgment is trustworthy habitually listens to what can be said against them and profits from just criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wise people collate their opinions with those of others, seek objections rather than avoid them, and expose their positions to all varieties of opinion. This habit strengthens rather than weakens reliable judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hear all sides to approximate full understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The only practical way to approach knowledge of a whole subject is to hear what persons of every variety of opinion can say about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To 'know only his own side of the case' is to know little of it. One must study all modes in which a subject can be looked at to approach understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal scope for free discussion (no protected sacred topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reasons for free discussion are sound, they must apply even to doctrines regarded as certain; forbidding questioning because something is 'so certain' assumes infallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is inconsistent to permit discussion of doubtful matters but exclude certain doctrines; declaring a proposition immune from questioning is to decide for others without hearing contrary views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of a belief is itself contestable
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguing that a belief should be protected from attack because it is useful merely shifts the need for discussion to a different question—utility is an opinion and requires debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot justify suppressing an opinion on grounds of usefulness without the same infallible authority you would need to condemn it as false. The truth of a belief is part of its utility; prohibiting truth-claims prevents fair debate about usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of truth-claims entails illegitimate authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventing people from defending the truth of an opinion (while perhaps allowing them to assert its utility) is inconsistent and effectively assumes the prohibitor's infallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either side must be able to argue both truth and utility; forbidding defence of truth undermines fair assessment and privileges received opinion unjustly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical warning: truth does not inevitably survive persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Persecution can and has successfully suppressed true opinions for long periods; truth does not automatically triumph over legal or social penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited examples: Reformation movements suppressed repeatedly before Luther, martyrs and persecuted reformers. Persecution may delay or extinguish truths for centuries; permitting free expression increases chances that truth will reappear and prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social stigma as effective suppression (chilling effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even absent legal penalties, social exclusion and stigma are powerful deterrents that prevent people from professing or propagating dissenting opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion from livelihood, ostracism, and reputational penalties can suppress opinions as effectively as imprisonment. This causes many to disguise beliefs or refrain from advocacy, weakening public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holding belief without understanding its grounds is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting a belief undoubtingly, without knowledge of grounds or ability to defend it, is not genuine understanding; such dogmatic assent is a superstition rather than reasoned truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education and public discourse should aim to teach the grounds and objections for important beliefs; unlike mathematics, controversial subjects always have meaningful opposing arguments that must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching controversial subjects requires exposure to opposing arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: On any subject where difference of opinion is possible, instruction should include the reasons on both sides so students can understand and defend their convictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematics is exceptional in lacking a wrong side; in morals, religion, and politics, three-fourths of arguments often consist in dispelling appearances favoring contrary opinions. Understanding requires studying adversarial cases (Cicero example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression damages both heretics and conformists
rubrics_metrics.description: Banning or stigmatizing dissent harms dissenters (who cannot defend and develop their views) and, perhaps more, those who are not heretics, by cowing their reason and narrowing intellectual development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include loss of moral courage, inward hypocrisy (public conformity, private dissent), and a decline in the number of open, fearless, logically consistent thinkers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of discussion cultivates an intellectually active people
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods of mental freedom (when authority's yoke is broken) correlate with intellectual and institutional improvements; free controversy is necessary for broad mental activity in a people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: effects of the Reformation, eighteenth-century continental speculation, and German intellectual ferment. Without open debate, a general atmosphere of mental slavery prevents widespread intellectual vigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalized adversarial testing strengthens convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices like appointing a 'devil's advocate' or allowing formal critique before conferring honors provide necessary testing of claims and prevent unexamined reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even most sacred persons or doctrines benefit from having objections aired (example: canonisation process allowing a devil's advocate). Openness to challenge is a safeguard against institutional errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal punishment for opinion presumes illegitimate judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Using law to punish opinion or its expression presupposes that authorities can infallibly decide which doctrines are harmful or true; this is an unjustifiable assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment for opinions both misjudges the possibility of truth and violates the need for public defence. Historical examples (Socrates, early Christians) show tragic consequences of legal suppression.
